source: Schmidt, Norman, Boshuizen (1990) A cognitive perspective on medical expertise: theory and implication
finding: Founding statement of the illness-script theory of expertise. Expertise is not better reasoning or deeper pathophysiology. It rests on stored structures that describe prototypical or real patients. Intermediate students instead use causal pathophysiological models.
numbers: Abstract only. Lists five phenomena the theory explains: content specificity, data-gathering differences, standard setting, decline on some measures with expertise, errors linked to longer response times in visual diagnosis.
quote: contain relatively little knowledge about pathophysiological causes of symptoms and complaints but a wealth of clinically relevant information
limits: Abstract only; full paper behind a paywall. The theory is a review-and-proposal, not one experiment.
agent_relevance: The class library should hold per-disease structures rich in context and consequences, not long causal chains.

source: Schmidt and Rikers (2007) How expertise develops in medicine: knowledge encapsulation and illness script formation
finding: Reviews 30 years of work. Biomedical knowledge becomes encapsulated under clinical labels, then reorganised into illness scripts. Most studies fit this view. Debate remains on the role of biomedical knowledge in case processing.
numbers: Abstract only; no sample numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Authors themselves say conflicting data exist.
agent_relevance: Two stage design for memory: causal detail stays retrievable but is hidden behind a label.

source: Schmidt and Mamede (2020) How cognitive psychology changed the face of medical education research
finding: Gives the staged account. Stage 1: causal networks from pathophysiology. Stage 2: encapsulation, where a label such as sepsis stands for a causal chain. Stage 3: narrative illness scripts, rich in enabling conditions and manifestations, poor in mechanism. Scripts range from disease prototypes to single remembered patients. Intermediate effect: students recall more than experts.
numbers: Experts used the label sepsis for a chain that students spelled out from contaminated syringes to symptoms (Schmidt 1988 as cited). No new sample numbers; it is a narrative review.
quote: Encapsulated knowledge is gradually reorganized into narrative structures that represent a patient with a particular disease
limits: Secondary source. Notes the debate: bias view says reasoning errors, knowledge view says knowledge deficits (Norman 2017).
agent_relevance: Maps onto the schema: a stored class with label, enabling conditions, manifestations. Keep mechanism only as a fallback.

source: Charlin, Boshuizen, Custers, Feltovich (2007) Scripts and clinical reasoning
finding: Script theory from cognitive psychology applied to medicine. A script is a goal-directed knowledge structure that yields expectations, checks features, and guides action. Raises how scripts develop and refine with experience.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Conceptual essay; no data. Script content is idiosyncratic to each clinician.
agent_relevance: Scripts predict features that should be present, so absence of an expected feature is a signal. Good fit for a check step.

source: Lubarsky, Dory, Audetat, Custers, Charlin (2015) Using script theory to cultivate illness script formation and clinical reasoning
finding: Defines the working loop: script activation from early cues, gauging fit between actual and expected features, instantiation (filling slots), and a continuum from rapid pattern recognition to slow analytic reasoning depending on script quality and situation. Node types: faults, enabling conditions, consequences.
numbers: No sample numbers; teaching-oriented synthesis.
quote: script instantiation describes the process of filling a script's empty 'slots'
limits: Review. Speed of processing depends on script quality, complexity, stakes and time.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete S2 representation: activate candidates, compare expected versus found features, fill slots. Switch to analytic work when fit is poor.

source: Charlin, Brailovsky, Leduc, Blouin (2000) The Script Concordance test: a tool to assess the reflective clinician
finding: Test built on script theory. Examinees interpret new data against a hypothesis and are scored for concordance with a panel of experts. Reported reliability, face and construct validity.
numbers: Abstract gives no figures.
limits: Abstract only. Scoring depends on panel quality and panel disagreement.
agent_relevance: A scoring idea: judge how new data shifts a hypothesis, compared with expert panel direction. Usable as a probe of an LLM class library.

source: Hobus, Schmidt, Boshuizen, Patel (1987) Contextual factors in the activation of first diagnostic hypotheses
finding: Experts used enabling conditions (age, sex, history, risk factors) from the patient picture and chart to generate first hypotheses. Novices used them less.
numbers: 18 experts and 17 novices; 32 case histories on three slides each. Experts produced almost 50% more correct hypotheses, and recalled more relevant context. Only experts showed a high correlation between diagnostic accuracy and recall.
limits: Small samples. Single Dutch setting. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Context cues set the first candidate list. The agent should read patient context before symptoms.

source: Brooks, Norman, Allen (1991) Role of specific similarity in a medical diagnostic task
finding: Rival to prototype scripts. Diagnosis of skin disorders was helped by seen similar cases, and more so than dissimilar cases in the same category. Effect held after a 2-week delay and across diagnostic procedures.
numbers: Three experiments with residents and general practitioners; the abstract gives no figures.
limits: Abstract only. Multiple-choice format that always contained the right answer.
agent_relevance: Retrieval by similarity to specific stored cases may matter as much as abstract classes. Keep worked cases as well as class summaries.

source: Norman, Young, Brooks (2007) Non-analytical models of clinical reasoning: the role of experience
finding: Non-analytic reasoning based on similarity to prior exemplars is a part of diagnosis at all levels, in dermatology, ECG and psychiatry. Retrieval is rapid and not open to introspection. Early hypotheses can lead to re-reading of findings.
numbers: Abstract only; reviews McMaster studies.
limits: Abstract only. Evidence is mostly from visual or short-vignette tasks.
agent_relevance: Early hypothesis can bias reading of later findings. Pair recall of cases with a de-biasing step. Fits the guardrail on doubt only on a signal.

source: Rikers, Schmidt, Boshuizen (2000) Knowledge encapsulation and the intermediate effect
finding: Neurologists diagnosed cardiology and pulmonology cases outside their field faster and more accurately than students. Recall and pathophysiology protocols showed an inverted U across expertise, while the share of encapsulating concepts rose with expertise.
numbers: Neurologists, 2nd-year and 6th-year students; four cases. 6th-year students recalled most. Inverted U in recall; rising proportion of encapsulating concepts.
limits: Abstract only. Group sizes not in abstract. Four cases.
agent_relevance: Recall of more detail is not skill. Do not score the agent on how much it lists; score on label quality.

source: Rikers, Loyens, te Winkel, Schmidt, Sins (2005) The role of biomedical knowledge in clinical reasoning: a lexical decision study
finding: Both physicians and students judged diagnostic target words faster and more accurately than biomedical ones, yet physicians were faster at both. Biomedical knowledge is still active in experts.
numbers: 15 family physicians, 20 fourth-year students; 60 clinical texts; reaction time and errors.
limits: Small sample. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Mechanism knowledge stays accessible behind labels. Keep it callable when the label fails.

source: de Bruin, Schmidt, Rikers (2005) The role of basic science knowledge and clinical knowledge in diagnostic reasoning: a structural equation modeling approach
finding: Of four causal models, the one with basic science integrated into clinical knowledge fit best. Models linking basic science directly to diagnosis fit poorly.
numbers: 59 family physicians invited, 44 (75%) responded; 184 students (100%) from years 2 to 6; Maastricht.
limits: One school, one curriculum. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Supports encapsulation: mechanism helps through clinical knowledge, not as a separate route.

source: Woods, Brooks, Norman (2007) It all makes sense: biomedical knowledge, causal connections and memory in the novice diagnostician
finding: Novices who learned causal mechanisms for artificial diseases kept diagnostic accuracy better over a week and relied more on causal information after a delay.
numbers: Experiment 1: 89% correct (causal) vs 78% (feature list) after a delay. Experiment 2: reliance on causal information 57% vs 43% mean probability.
limits: Artificial diseases, novices, short delay. Abstract only. Does not test experts.
agent_relevance: Boundary on the pure script view: mechanism acts as glue for recall of feature sets.

source: Woods, Brooks, Norman (2007) The role of biomedical knowledge in diagnosis of difficult clinical cases
finding: Novices taught causal mechanisms did better on cases with irrelevant findings and on unfamiliar terminology. In Experiment 2 (one week later) the benefit held for unfamiliar terminology.
numbers: Two experiments; the abstract gives no figures.
limits: Artificial diseases; abstract only.
agent_relevance: On hard or odd cases, mechanism knowledge helps. Use mechanism as the fallback when script match fails.

source: Coderre, Mandin, Harasym, Fick (2003) Diagnostic reasoning strategies and diagnostic success
finding: In gastroenterology think-aloud, pattern recognition and scheme-inductive reasoning had greater odds of success than hypothetico-deductive reasoning. Expertise and case also predicted success.
numbers: Logistic regression on think-aloud protocols; the abstract gives no odds ratios.
limits: Abstract only. Four presentations in one specialty.
agent_relevance: Recognition from organised schemes beat hypothesis testing; test the agent recognition-first path against an explore-first path.

source: Devantier, Minda, Goldszmidt, Haddad (2009) Categorizing patients in a forced-choice triad task
finding: Experts matched patients on deep features (management category) more than novices. Residents did not differ from experts.
numbers: Invited 130 novices, 11 intermediates, 159 endocrinologists; completers 15, 11 and 8. Novices vs experts t(68) = -3.63, p = .0006; intermediates vs experts t(68) = -0.24, p = .81. Years in practice correlated with diagnostic triads r = .39, p = .02, not management triads r = .17.
limits: Very low completion; 10-item task; self-selected experts.
agent_relevance: Categories can be built on management, not only disease. A class library may need action-based classes.

source: Keemink, Custers, van Dijk, Ten Cate (2018) Illness script development in pre-clinical education through case-based clinical reasoning training
finding: After a case-based course, students had richer scripts for course diseases and diagnosed them better. Gains were in enabling conditions rather than fault knowledge.
numbers: 32 students, within-subject. Script richness 14.47 (SD 3.25) vs 12.14 (SD 2.80), p<0.001, about 20% higher. Diagnostic score 1.63 (SD 0.32) vs 1.15 (SD 0.29), p<0.001. Exam correlation with recognition r = 0.571.
limits: Small sample; non-randomised choice of diseases; short term.
agent_relevance: Richness of enabling conditions predicts recognition. Measure script quality by that, as a probe for the agent.

source: Norman, Monteiro, Sherbino, Ilgen, Schmidt, Mamede (2017) The causes of errors in clinical reasoning
finding: Both fast and slow processes cause error. Bias induction is easy to show in the lab, but its real share of errors is not well shown. Teaching bias recognition does not reduce errors. Reorganising knowledge gives small but consistent benefit.
numbers: Abstract only; no figures.
limits: Abstract only. Contested by the bias-focused camp.
agent_relevance: Fix knowledge organisation before adding bias checks.

source: Yazdani and Hoseini Abardeh (2019) Five decades of research and theorization on clinical reasoning: a critical review
finding: Sorts theories into process models (hypothetico-deductive) and knowledge-structure models (illness script, pattern recognition/exemplar, schema). Lists criticisms of hypothetico-deductive work: it does not separate novice from expert and is not sequential in practice.
numbers: Review table of theories; no experiments.
limits: Narrative review; low detail on effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Shows scripts, exemplars and schemes as rival formats; the class library can hold more than one.

source: Illness scripts in nursing: directed content analysis (2022) J Adv Nurs
finding: Illness script components apply in nursing, and five new components (management, boundary, impact, occurrence, explicative) were proposed.
numbers: 3912 statements from expert nurses thinking aloud on 20 patient problems.
limits: Qualitative; abstract only; nurses not physicians.
agent_relevance: Script slots may need action and boundary fields beyond fault, enabling conditions and consequences.

source: Kanjee, Crowe, Rodman (2023) Accuracy of a generative AI model in a complex diagnostic challenge
finding: GPT-4 on NEJM clinicopathologic conference cases. Correct diagnosis in the differential in 64% of cases; top diagnosis in 39%.
numbers: 70 of 80 cases analysed. 45/70 (64%) in differential, 27/70 (39%) top. Mean differential 9.0 diagnoses. Mean rank of correct item 2.5. Scorer agreement 66%, kappa 0.57.
limits: Educational cases, not real encounters; some data left out of prompts; subjective scoring; possible training-set exposure. Read through a page summary tool, not the raw PDF.
agent_relevance: Recall of 64% against top-1 of 39% suggests ranking, not retrieval, is the weak point once the class is on the list.

source: Savage, Nayak, Gallo, Rangan, Chen (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for LLM interpretability in medicine (GPT-3.5)
finding: Prompts modelled on clinician reasoning modes were tested on MedQA free-response. For GPT-3.5, intuitive reasoning matched chain-of-thought; analytic, differential diagnosis and Bayesian prompts were worse.
numbers: GPT-3.5: chain-of-thought 46%, zero-shot 31%, intuitive 48% (p=0.4), analytic 40% (p=0.001), differential diagnosis 38% (p<0.001), Bayesian 42% (p=0.02).
limits: Free-response MedQA subset; older model; prompts only.
agent_relevance: Forcing a differential list did not help a weak model. Intuitive, recognition-first prompting did no harm.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts (GPT-4 on MedQA)
finding: For GPT-4 none of the clinical-reasoning prompts beat chain-of-thought significantly.
numbers: 498 questions after 20 API errors. Chain-of-thought 76%, intuitive 77% (p=0.73), analytic 78% (p=0.35), differential diagnosis 78% (p=0.24), Bayesian 72% (p=0.07).
limits: Not powered to find small gains; confidence intervals span about +/-5 points.
agent_relevance: Prompting the model to imitate clinician modes gives interpretability without loss, but no gain in accuracy.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts (GPT-4 on NEJM challenge cases)
finding: On hard NEJM cases the differential-diagnosis prompt was no better, nominally worse.
numbers: Chain-of-thought 38% vs differential diagnosis 34%; difference -4.2% (95% CI -11.4 to +2.1), p = 0.09.
limits: Single run; wide interval.
agent_relevance: Do not assume that listing candidates improves hard-case accuracy.

source: Goh et al. (2024) Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial
finding: Physicians given GPT-4 did not reason better than those with conventional resources. The model alone scored higher than both physician groups.
numbers: 50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents); up to 6 vignettes in 60 minutes. Median score 76% (LLM) vs 74% (conventional), adjusted difference 2 points (95% CI -4 to 8, p=.60). Time 519 vs 565 seconds (p=.20). LLM alone +16 points (95% CI 2 to 30, p=.03).
limits: Small sample; vignette task; clinicians not trained in prompting.
agent_relevance: The model own recall of disease classes is strong; the weak link is how its output is used.

source: Takita et al. (2025) Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic performance of generative AI versus physicians
finding: Across 83 studies, pooled generative-AI diagnostic accuracy was modest. It matched non-expert physicians and trailed experts.
numbers: 18,371 records screened, 83 included. Pooled accuracy 52.1% (95% CI 47.0 to 57.1). Versus non-experts difference 0.6% (95% CI -14.5 to 15.7, p=0.93). Versus experts 15.8% worse (95% CI 4.4 to 27.1, p=0.007). Most studies at high risk of bias.
limits: Heterogeneous tasks and models; GPT-4 most common; high risk of bias.
agent_relevance: The gap to experts is a gap in organised knowledge and use of cues. A class library targets it.

source: Moell, Sand Aronsson, Akbar (2025) Medical reasoning in LLMs: an in-depth analysis of DeepSeek R1
finding: A reasoning model reached 93% on 100 MedQA cases. The seven errors included anchoring and little consideration of alternatives. Longer reasoning went with more errors. The paper names script theory as a standard LLM reasoning should be checked against.
numbers: 100 MedQA cases; 93% accuracy; 7 error cases; reasoning under about 5,000 characters strongly linked to accuracy.
limits: Small sample; MedQA is exam-style and may be in training data; the length threshold is exploratory.
agent_relevance: Long reasoning as an uncertainty sign fits the doubt-only-on-a-signal guardrail. Anchoring is the script-activation failure.

source: Sim and Chen (2025) Critique of impure reason: unveiling the reasoning behaviour of medical LLMs
finding: Argues that medical benchmarks mix knowledge recall with reasoning, and no medical equivalent of ARC-AGI exists to isolate reasoning from stored knowledge.
numbers: No figures used here; read only the relevant passages, not the whole paper.
limits: Position paper.
agent_relevance: Scoring a recognition-based agent needs held-out cases where recall of classes cannot carry the answer.

source: Lilamand et al. (2026) How different versions of ChatGPT align with expert opinions on geriatric script concordance tests
finding: Direct script concordance test of LLMs. GPT-4 and 5 reached expert-like scores; GPT-3.5 did not; GPT-4o slightly lower.
numbers: 20 validated items, 43 experts. GPT-3.5 8/20 (15% majority alignment); GPT-4 15.6/20 and GPT-5 15.2/20 (45% alignment); GPT-4o 13.6/20.
limits: Abstract only; 20 items; one specialty.
agent_relevance: SCT is a ready probe of whether a model class library updates hypotheses like experts do.

source: Hudon et al. (2024) Using ChatGPT in Psychiatry to Design Script Concordance Tests
finding: ChatGPT-made SCTs were rated like expert-made ones, with a tendency to caricature.
numbers: 102 respondents; scenario P=.84, questions P=.99, expert opinion P=.07; 3 ChatGPT vs 3 expert SCTs.
limits: Only 6 SCTs; abstract only; tests item writing, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: LLMs can write script-style probes, but caricatured cases bias a class library.

source: Yapici Coskun, Kiyak, Coskun (2025) LLMs for generating SCT in obstetrics and gynecology: ChatGPT and Claude
finding: Both models wrote SCT items judged acceptable; difficulty was the weakest criterion.
numbers: 16 panelists, 11 criteria. Overall agreement 90.57% (GPT-4o) and 91.48% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet). Difficulty fit 71.25% and 76.25%.
limits: Abstract only; five topics.
agent_relevance: Item writing is not diagnosing.
